assessment.nobel_worthiness: The magic-wavelength optical lattice clock is a measurement breakthrough of the kind I value most: it combines Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation with the statistics of many atoms, taking fractional uncertainty to the 1e-18 level and below. It has enabled relativistic geodesy, tests of constancy of constants, searches for dark-matter signatures and a path to redefining the second. Laser stabilization (long coherence, ultrastable cavities) was part of the same story, and I know how demanding that is experimentally.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated the first Sr lattice clock; Ye drove it to record accuracy and stability, including the many-body and spin-polarized Sr systems. The two-name configuration is clean. Others (Lemonde, Takamoto, Hall and Hansch via the comb/laser stabilization) are outside the supplied credit, so any prize would implicitly leave out contributions that the committee would need to reason about separately.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST) have reproduced and surpassed the original performance, and the clocks are in operation as secondary representations of the second. Highly mature, the impact is demonstrated, and the timing is good given that the comb was recognized in 2005.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views the work as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and from Hall's earlier laser stabilization.
Whether Ye's work on ultracold molecules and his clock work might be preferred as one combined recognition; the supplied credit is limited to two people for this candidate.
Exact priority between Katori's proposal and early Sr lattice demonstrations by other groups (e.g. SYRTE, JILA) is from memory and not independently checked.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made superconducting qubits controllable and readable through dispersive coupling to microwave resonators, and thereby the platform behind present-day quantum processors, quantum-limited amplification and microwave-photon experiments. It is a clear case of a new measurement and control paradigm with large downstream impact. The conceptual step (strong coupling of a single artificial atom to a single photon in a resonator) is simple and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Blais (with Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf) wrote the 2004 theoretical proposal; Wallraff and Schoelkopf demonstrated strong coupling experimentally. Girvin is a plausible additional theorist not in the supplied credit, and the credit overlaps with the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits (Clarke, Devoret, Martinis), which complicates the story. The three supplied names are defensible.
assessment.maturity: Very strong and independent confirmation in many groups and companies; transmon-based devices are used worldwide. Timing is reasonable, though the 2025 prize may reduce urgency in the circuit area.
uncertainties: Overlap with the recent prize for superconducting circuits and whether the committee will see this as a distinct discovery.
Whether Devoret, Girvin or Nakamura should figure in attribution (outside the supplied credit).
Quantum advantage and fault tolerance are not yet established, which for some members makes the application impact still prospective.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions, followed by experimental realization of high-fidelity gates, entanglement of many ions and quantum algorithms, established a precision-controlled, long-coherence platform for quantum information. Trapped ions remain among the best qubits and are connected to the metrology of ion clocks. The experimental demonstrations are impressive and well documented.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the original proposal (1995); Blatt realized many of the key gates and algorithms in Innsbruck. Wineland and Monroe are major experimental contributors, and Wineland already received the 2012 prize for ion control, so the supplied three-name configuration is plausible but leaves Monroe and others uncited. B035 appears to overlap strongly with this entry; I rank only this one.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation from NIST, Oxford, Innsbruck, Maryland and industry. Mature, though scalable error-corrected computing is still to be demonstrated.
uncertainties: The relationship to the 2012 Wineland recognition and the weight of Monroe and Wineland in the experimental implementation.
B035 is close to a duplicate and could split support; the committee would need to decide on one framing.
Whether quantum computing as a whole is ready for a prize or should wait for stronger application demonstrations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Single colour-centre spins (NV centres in diamond and relatives) combine optical addressing with long room-temperature spin coherence, giving nanoscale magnetic, electric and temperature sensing, quantum registers and spin-photon interfaces. As a solid-state experimentalist working with optically addressed spins in crystals, I find this physically close to my own field and I value its sensing impact, including in biology and materials.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup demonstrated optical detection of single NV spins (1997); Awschalom pioneered spin coherence and control in semiconductors and colour centres; Lukin contributed major sensing and network demonstrations and theory. Walsworth, Jelezko, Hanson and Dutt are also major contributors, so allocation is contested and a three-person limit forces difficult exclusions. I choose the three above on originality of the central discoveries and breadth.
assessment.maturity: Widely reproduced across the world and moving into commercial sensing. Sensing is mature, whereas networks and computing are less so; there is a compound discovery here.
uncertainties: Compound discovery: single-spin detection, coherent control, and sensing may deserve different attribution.
Lukin also appears in other candidate entries, which complicates a combined prize design.
Priority and role of Jelezko, Hanson and Walsworth are from memory and not verified here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realize clean, tunable Hubbard models, enabled by the proposal of Jaksch et al. and by the superfluid-Mott transition (Greiner et al. 2002), and later single-site quantum gas microscopy. This provides a new way of observing many-body quantum matter with direct access to correlations, a genuine measurement advance.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch, Cirac, Gardiner) proposed the Hubbard realization; Bloch and Greiner demonstrated the Mott transition and developed microscopy. Hansch/Esslinger and Cirac are also reasonable. Zoller appears under several entries, which affects overall prize design, but credit here is clear for the three chosen.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed and extended by many groups. Mature as a field; real quantum simulation advantage on open problems is still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2001 BEC prize and Zoller's presence in multiple candidates.
Whether quantum simulation has produced a decisive solution to a major open physics problem yet.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable Rydberg-atom tweezer arrays give tens to hundreds of individually controlled neutral-atom qubits with strong, switchable interactions, demonstrating exotic phases, quantum simulation and high-fidelity gates and error-correction steps. The experimental advance over the last decade is rapid and clearly important.
assessment.attribution: Saffman and Zoller (blockade-gate proposals, with Jaksch/Lukin), Lukin's group at Harvard (51/256-atom simulators), Browaeys (Institut d'Optique tweezer arrays) and others are central; I omit Zoller because he appears in other entries and his role here is proposal-level. Atom Computing, Bakr, Endres and Browaeys-Lahaye are overlapping; allocation is disputed.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly advancing, with several independent groups confirming; interpretation of what is a durable, fundamental discovery is not yet stable, so I regard it as somewhat premature.
uncertainties: Premature relative to the older platforms; fault tolerance is still being demonstrated.
Attribution among Lukin, Browaeys, Saffman, Bernien, Endres, Bakr and Zoller is contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution turned quantum measurement and entanglement into a security protocol, now implemented over fibre and satellite links. Conceptually original (BB84, E91), and experiments (including satellite links) demonstrate real devices, but practical impact is still limited by rates, distance and side-channel security.
assessment.attribution: BB84 (Bennett and Brassard) and E91 (Ekert) are clear theoretical sources; Jian-Wei Pan is the leading experimentalist for satellite and network demonstrations, but with a three-person cap, theory-only recognition would underweight experiment. The 2022 prize already recognized Bell tests, which touches the foundation of E91, so the allocation needs care.
assessment.maturity: Protocols are mature and commercial systems exist; global quantum networks are still developing and practical security is debated.
uncertainties: Real-world security and impact are unproven at scale.
Overlap with the 2022 prize on entanglement experiments.
Whether theory-only recognition (without Pan) is considered appropriate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling mechanical oscillators to their quantum ground state and demonstrating quantum-limited readout, squeezing and entanglement of macroscopic mechanical modes extends the quantum regime to massive objects and sets limits for precision force and displacement sensing, which connects to gravitational-wave detection and transducers. I value the measurement relevance.
assessment.attribution: The field has five credited names, and the key milestones (sideband cooling, ground-state cooling, strong coupling, quantum-limited measurement) are split between several groups; Cleland and Teufel in electromechanics, Painter, Kippenberg and Aspelmeyer in optomechanics. Any three-name selection is arbitrary to some degree.
assessment.maturity: Independent reproductions across platforms exist, but applications such as transducers are still developing, so the field is somewhat early for recognition.
uncertainties: Difficult attribution among five or more groups.
Practical impact and fundamental surprise are limited so far compared with the higher-ranked candidates.
